questions.question: 'Women in India face discrimination, disadvantages and oppression in many ways.' Highlight any two aspects of life where you witness this inequality.
answer_steps: Any one: education: the literacy rate among women is only 54% compared with 76% among men, and parents prefer to spend on sons' education; or jobs: few women hold highly paid and valued jobs, and their work is not valued.

Any other one: women are paid less than men for the same work despite the Equal Wages Act; son preference and sex-selective abortion have lowered the child sex ratio; women face exploitation at work and domestic violence at home.

questions.question: Mention different aspects of life in which women are discriminated or disadvantaged in India.
answer_steps: Education: the literacy rate among women is only 54% against 76% for men, and fewer girls go for higher studies.

Work and pay: women are a small share of highly paid jobs, work about an hour more than men daily but their work is unpaid and unvalued, and they are paid less despite the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.
Son preference has lowered the child sex ratio to 919; women face harassment, exploitation and domestic violence, and their representation in legislatures is low.

questions.question: State different forms of communal politics with one example each.
answer_steps: Everyday beliefs: religious prejudices and stereotypes, such as believing one's religion is superior; and the quest for political dominance, such as majoritarian dominance or the demand for a separate state for a minority.
Political mobilisation on religious lines: use of sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and fear, for example appeals to voters of one religion at election time.
Communal violence, riots and massacres: for example the riots at the time of Partition in 1947.

questions.question: State how caste inequalities are still continuing in India.
answer_steps: Most people still marry within their own caste or tribe.
Untouchability has not ended completely, despite constitutional prohibition.
Castes that had access to education did well, while others lagged behind; so upper castes are over-represented in the urban middle class, and caste is still linked to economic status.

questions.question: State two reasons to say that caste alone cannot determine election results in India.
answer_steps: No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste, so candidates need the support of many castes; and no party wins the votes of all voters of a caste.
Ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose elections, and voters judge the government's performance and the popularity of leaders.

questions.question: What is the status of women's representation in India's legislative bodies?
answer_steps: It is low: women were about 14 per cent of the Lok Sabha in 2019 (about 13.6 per cent in 2024), and less than 5 per cent in many state assemblies.

In panchayats and municipalities one-third of seats are reserved for women, giving more than 10 lakh women representatives; a 2023 Act will reserve one-third of Lok Sabha and assembly seats after the next census and delimitation.

questions.question: Mention any two constitutional provisions that make India a secular state.
answer_steps: There is no official religion for the Indian state; and the Constitution gives everyone freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not follow any.
The Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, and allows the state to intervene to ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability.

questions.question: What were the demands of feminist movements?
answer_steps: Extension of voting rights to women, and enhancing their political and legal status.
Improving educational and career opportunities; radical movements also demanded equality in personal and family life.

questions.question: Give two examples of religion in politics that are NOT communal.

Human rights groups demanding protection of religious minorities, or women's movements demanding fair family laws in all religions.

questions.question: How has politics changed caste ('politics in caste')?
answer_steps: Each caste group tries to become bigger by incorporating neighbouring castes or sub-castes, and castes enter coalitions with other castes.
New kinds of caste groups, such as 'backward' and 'forward' castes, have emerged in politics.

questions.question: Explain the features of India's secular state.
answer_steps: There is no official religion for the Indian state, unlike Buddhism in Sri Lanka, Islam in Pakistan and Christianity in England.
The Constitution gives all individuals and communities freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not to follow any, and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.
The state can intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability.

questions.question: What are the positive and negative effects of caste in politics?
answer_steps: Positive: caste politics has given Dalit and OBC castes better access to decision making, and one-person-one-vote brought new consciousness among castes earlier treated as inferior.
Negative: exclusive attention to caste can divert attention from pressing issues like poverty, development and corruption.
Negative: caste division can lead to tensions, conflict and even violence.

questions.question: Why is the representation of women in legislatures important? How has India tried to improve it?
answer_steps: When women are poorly represented, issues of their well-being do not get adequate attention; women were only about 14% of the Lok Sabha in 2019.
One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women, and there are now more than 10 lakh women representatives in local bodies.
The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 will reserve one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women after the next census and delimitation.

questions.question: What is communalism? Explain the various forms that communalism can take in politics.
answer_steps: Communalism is the use of religion in politics in exclusive and partisan terms, based on the belief that religion is the principal basis of social community and that followers of one religion have the same interests.
Everyday beliefs: religious prejudices, stereotypes of religious communities and belief in the superiority of one's religion.
Quest for political dominance: majoritarian dominance for the majority community, or a desire for a separate political unit for a minority community.
Political mobilisation on religious lines: use of sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and plain fear, such as appeals to voters of one religion in elections.
Communal violence, riots and massacres: India and Pakistan suffered some of the worst communal riots at the time of Partition, and there has also been communal violence after independence.

questions.question: 'Caste has not disappeared from contemporary India.' Explain. Also show why caste alone cannot decide election results.
answer_steps: Most people still marry within their own caste, and untouchability has not ended completely despite the constitutional ban.
Groups that had access to education did well, so upper castes are over-represented in the urban middle class, and caste remains linked to economic status.
But no parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste, so every candidate needs the support of many castes and communities.
No party gets all the votes of a caste, and many parties put up candidates from the same caste.

Ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose; voters judge the government's performance and the popularity of leaders, and people of the same caste vote differently depending on their economic condition.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"The result of this division of labour is that although women constitute half of the humanity, their role in public life, especially politics, is minimal in most societies. Earlier, only men were allowed to participate in public affairs, vote and contest for public offices. Gradually the gender issue was raised in politics. Women in different parts of the world organised and agitated for equal rights."* (NCERT)

(i) Which division of labour is referred to here? (1)

(ii) Who is a feminist? (1)

(iii) Give two ways in which women are disadvantaged in India today. (2)
answer_steps: (i) The sexual division of labour, in which all work inside the home is done or organised by women.
(ii) A woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.

(iii) Any two: lower literacy (54% against 76%); few women in highly paid jobs; lower wages for the same work; son preference and a falling child sex ratio; harassment and domestic violence; low representation in legislatures.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"Communalism was and continues to be one of the major challenges to democracy in our country. The makers of our Constitution were aware of this challenge. That is why they chose the model of a secular state. This choice was reflected in several constitutional provisions."* (NCERT)

(i) Why is communalism a challenge to democracy? (1)

(ii) Name any one country that gives special status to a religion. (1)

(iii) State two constitutional provisions that make India secular. (2)
answer_steps: (i) It treats religion as the basis of the nation and pits followers of one religion against another, which can lead to domination and violence.
(ii) Any one: Sri Lanka (Buddhism), Pakistan (Islam), England (Christianity).

(iii) Any two: no official religion; freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion; no discrimination on grounds of religion; state intervention to ensure equality within religions, such as the ban on untouchability.
